newsitem.title: USA: Mars rover back on track after computer glitches.
newsitem.headline: Mars rover back on track after computer glitches.

text.p: The little Mars space buggy Sojourner was back on track on Tuesday after being hit by a series of computer glitches that gave it the weekend off.
"It was an excellent day on Mars," said Pathfinder Project Scientist Matthew Golombek. "The rover did a great job."

Mars, like Earth, might have foggy mornings, one of the project's scientists said, adding to the evidence that the Red Planet contains water and could have given birth to primitive forms of life billions of years ago.
Scientists excitedly discussed the rover's latest rock analysis, on a boulder dubbed "Yogi," saying it proved more like an earth rock than the previously analysed "Barnacle Bill."

At a media briefing at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory here, James Greenwood, a minerologist from the University of Tennessee and a member of the Pathfinder science team, said "Yogi" was "more earth like than we expected to find" and appeared to be older than "Barnacle Bill."
Greenwood said "Yogi" contained more magnesium than "Barnacle Bill," adding, "generally that means it is the more primitive of the two rocks."
Golombek said the computer problems that "bedeviled" the mission late last week and over the weekend, had "impacted us severely," putting the Sojourner several days behind in its rock sampling tasks.

But he stressed the six-wheeled rover, which is about the size of a micorwave oven, could operate on the Martian surface "indefinitely" and its mission had already been extended to a long term project, meaning that it would return more data to Earth than had originally been planned.

Computer scientist Glen Reeves explained that the computer on board the Pathfinder landing craft had reset itself three times when it sensed an overload, automatically cutting communications with Earth.

This was the result of a built-in safety measure in the software programme. "An analogy would be when your PC (personal computer) locks up and you reach around the back and hit the reset button," Reeves said.

He said his team was looking at ways of altering the software from the ground but in the meantime the problem had been overcome by asking the computer to perform only one task at a time, instead of multiple functions.

Scientists early on Monday also received pictures from the lander for their so-called "Superpan," -- a 12-colour, 360-degree panorama of the Martian surface as seen by the lander's camera, stretching from the lander to the horizon.

In further evidence that Mars contains water, meteorologist Tim Schofield said a weather station aboard the lander had detected shifts in temperature changes that his team believed were caused by fog.

He said that the night and early morning cooling pattern, when the temperatures at the planet's surface drop from their daytime highs of about 7 degrees Farenheit (-13 degrees Centigrade) to minus 100 F had been interrupted on a number of occasions and failed to reach the normal lows.
"We think this might be caused by water in the atmosphere condensing as fog near the surface and changing the cooling pattern," he said.

Steven Lee, an astronomer on the orbiting Hubble telescope team that is working with the Pathfinder scientists, said the Hubble had detected clouds on Mars about nine miles (15 kms) above the planet's surface.
